tur74-1: In England, NICE’s 2025 guideline recommends talking with people at risk of falling about what to do after a fall and how to get up from the floor. Trying the steps in advance, with someone beside you, makes it easier to know what to do if you really do fall. In a study that followed 110 people over 90 for a year, 80% of those who fell could not get up without help after at least one fall, and 30% stayed on the floor for an hour or longer; lying on the floor for a long time was linked with serious injury, hospital admission and moving into a care home. Although call alarms were common, they were not used in most of the falls that led to a long time on the floor.
tur74-2: In a study done at home, participants chose their depth by how hard it felt, and after 4 weeks an average fall of 9 mmHg in systolic blood pressure was measured. The target: by the end of each of the 4 rounds, an effort of about 4, 5.5, 7 and 8.5 out of 10, respectively. In other words, the first round feels comfortable and the last is hard but manageable.
tur74-3: Stay at the same height for all four rounds; the effort is expected to rise from round to round. If the effort in the last round was clearly below or above the target, start slightly lower or higher in your next session.

tur74-5: In the Cochrane review of 16 randomised controlled trials (1,058 children), no significant difference in pain after one year was found between custom-made insoles, ready-made insoles and shoes alone in children with painless flat feet; however, each comparison rests on a single trial (106–108 children) and the certainty of the evidence is low. The authors state that they found no evidence supporting costly custom insoles for healthy children without pain. Insoles may help in conditions where the foot is painful, such as juvenile arthritis.
tur74-6: One of the most common causes of flat feet appearing in adulthood is strain and weakening of the tendon that runs behind the inner ankle bone to the sole of the foot and holds the arch up (tibialis posterior). In a study of 36 people with an early-stage problem of this tendon, 12 weeks of resistance exercises added to insoles improved pain and function more than insoles and stretching alone. The risk rises with age; it is more common in middle-aged women. Excess weight, diabetes, inflammatory arthritis and a blow or sprain to the area set the scene.
tur74-7: Yes. The tissues of the foot can stretch through injury, ageing or excess weight; in adults one common cause is weakening of the tendon that runs behind the inner ankle and holds the arch. See a doctor if you did not have flat feet before, or if only one foot is affected.
